en: There dwells a certain mendicant who collects ten indeclinables; we beg him for the pair of indeclinables "na mama" (not mine)—what else is there? The *Vairāgyaśataka* composed by the illustrious Appayadīkṣita.
There dwells a certain mendicant who gathers ten indeclinables;
This empire known as dispassion (*vairāgya*) has wisdom for its counselor, the power of fortitude, the subduing of all volitions, and peace as its wealth; its domain is the three worlds. (AppVs 2)
The world fears kings, and kings in turn fear their enemies;
but the kingdom of one free from desire is fearless from all sides, even from Brahmā down to the God of Death.
Alms-givers are mothers, parents are teachers, children are disciples;
for one who is detached, tranquility is the beloved wife, being the cause of solitary delight.
Those who do not perform any action because they are free from both what is to be done and its opposite—they alone are liberated; Gautama is the witness to this doubt.
Let the sky fall, let the earth split asunder, let the mountains move, or let the oceans collide;
let the world be turned upside down—what loss is there for one who is free from passion?
Who are the thieves? Who are the backbiters? Who are the enemies? And who are the kinsmen?
The entire world is under the control of him whose mind is under control. (AppVs 7)
Let objects present themselves, or let the senses merge with their objects;
if the single internal organ is at peace, what concern can there be then? // AppVs_8 //
Why should the ignorant dwell in the caves of Mount Meru in order to avoid sense objects?
For lotuses do not grow upon the elements unless they are moistened by water.

In this disease of existence, ignorance is the primary cause; birth itself is the premonitory symptom; wandering through cyclic existence is the progression of the illness; and ultimate peace is the medicine.
Like a human being who remembers his birth as a pig, the wise person, loathing from afar the object he himself once enjoyed, cultivates dispassion.
Just as childhood does not please one in youth, nor youth in old age, so too the restless activity of desire does not please the wise when they have attained tranquility.
Having examined sense objects hundreds of times, some who are worthy of offering immediately abandon them here and there;
others, like crows that eat vomit, continue to pursue those very same things.

The parents are the last [to be left behind], the wife and children are the last; how is it that the wise become dispassionate here, even while there is still affection for those who must be cared for? AppVs_14 //
Fickle people wander about like blades of grass when the fierce wind called "woman" blows;
yet the virtuous, like mountains that support the earth, do not tremble at all in its presence.

Those who are virtuous and relish the taste of the bliss of tranquility hold sensual pleasure— in which worldly people find the highest enjoyment— to be loathsome, just as those who feed on nectar view the food of pigs.
Those who possess only a slight degree of distraction, yet have reached the pinnacle of expanded knowledge,
perceive even their own actions as if they were those of another.
The wise follow fools who are attached to the improper and find satisfaction only in what is improper,
just as parents follow their playing children.
Just as trees nourish a man with water while simultaneously robbing him of their flowers and fruit,
so do the virtuous behave equally toward both those who benefit them and those who harm them.

The discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal exists for everyone in the case of a jar and "jar-ness"; that [discrimination] which brings about peace is true discrimination, while all other [notions] are merely non-discrimination.
Just as a youth proceeds at the proper time toward sensual pleasure not yet attained,
so too does some rare individual proceed toward the bliss of Brahman by the power of fortune.
One seeking liberation should consider the virtues of sons in the matter of independence, the virtues of wives at the time of taking a second wife,
and the virtues of brothers regarding the rules of inheritance.
Even for the sake of that person who asks, "What is my destination? regarding their own welfare even at the moment of their final breath, the wicked commit evil deeds.
They quarrel with their fathers while teaching their sons devotion to the father;
they study the scriptures while violating the wives of others.
Peace is unattainable, cessation results in unworthiness, there is a turning away from receiving gifts,
and patience is weak— these are the qualities of desistance in the Kali age.
There are those who know policy, those who know destiny, and there are even those who know the Vedas;
those who know the scriptures and those who know Brahman can also be found, but those who know the knowledge of their own ignorance are rare.
How can the world attain straightforwardness when one's own mind is turbid with the Kali age?
While a defect in the eye persists, how could the appearance of two moons ever cease?
Effort should be made to harmonize the objects with the heart of the subject;
for who becomes happy by applying medicine to the object while leaving the eye untreated?
Wives are devoted to their sons, and sons are preoccupied with seizing their father’s wealth;
when one has gone to the next world, the mother is left as a refuge for weeping—what then is a kinsman?

They see those who are dying and infer from them those who will die; they remember those who have died and speak of them as if they were still present, acting toward the Supreme as if it were eternal.
The deluded quarrel over who will be the guarantor for tomorrow morning;
yet on this very night, who is the guarantor for one's own existence?
Canals have been made wide, walls have been built with stones, and powerful buffaloes have been purchased; thus they think, "We have accomplished our purpose. (AppVs 32)

Even the water of the Gaṅgā is as futile upon a body that is internally fouled by the impurities of the Kali age— as useless as a handful of darbha grass poured into a jar of liquor— reaching from the feet to the head.
How can people nourish that very body which ought to be punished for the sake of pleasure?
For those desiring sugar do not revere the stalks of the sugarcane.
Generally, the mind of a living being becomes deluded at the moment of the departure of the vital breath;
if it is not deluded by virtue, one dies while thinking only of one's sons.
Those who immerse themselves in the ocean called saṃsāra to extinguish the fire of their bellies do not provide fire in their own homes to alleviate the pain of the cold.
Wealth, when acquired and then renounced, produces the appearance of happiness;
when renounced utterly, it conduces to supreme bliss.
Excessive wealth is destroyed either by the king or by thieves;
indeed, when food is consumed in excess, there will be either vomiting or purging.
He bows down, soothes, prostrates, and wanders about constantly;
like a man possessed by a *piśācī*, he has fallen under the power of craving.
Parents [are dear] due to the unseen force of procreation; sons and even sons-in-law [are dear] due to the unseen force of death;
and kinsmen [are dear] due to the unseen force of strife—once this is determined, what more remains to be desired?
Since he himself performs daily those very acts for his father’s sake in the next world, let this serve as an analogy;
is it not sufficient to produce dispassion toward one's own son?
When poverty has not receded, what characteristic of its departure have you observed?
If the world, up to the four-faced Brahmā, remains wretched due to the non-fulfillment of desire, [then what sign of its end is seen]?
Indeed, wealth is not a genus; whatever one desires is itself that person's wealth.
Just as various things [are considered wealth] for commoners, so too is the state of possessing nothing (ākiñcanya) the wealth of the wise.
If craving is accepted, then the entire world must also be accepted;
if peace is accepted, then even one's own self does not belong to oneself.
That which subdues the donor, which conciliates his attendants,
and for which he feels no shame— whose equal is that gain of inner disposition?
What effort is required to fill a belly the size of a span?
Must even a lake be sounded out in order to drink a handful of water?
How utterly deluded are those who, while half a watch passes in preparation and two watches pass in fasting—both clearly manifest—still remain attached to physical beauty! (AppVs 47)
They call a young woman barren and abandon one who has many sons as being old;
they revile one who has few children—what kind of wife is pleasing to those full of desire?
Those who have not taken a wife go to grief; those who have taken two wives do not [go to grief];
we see no men satisfied with women who think, "These are the wives of others. AppVs_49 //
In carrying out the command of Madana, I consider this entire world to be of one single form;
the distinction as "animals," "humans," or "gods" arises from nothing else.
The place for the release of semen is somewhat like the place for the discharge of excrement and urine;
ordained by fate as "women," how many people here plunge into it?
"Having studied the Vedas according to the rules and having reflected upon their meaning, one must take a wife"—who uttered this joke? AppVs_52 //
Wicked women are acquired with great hardship, guarded, and cherished day by day; yet those deluded fools enjoy them for a pleasure that is devoid of virtue.
Eat, drink, taste, stay awake, lie down, or stand;
even for a single moment during the day, reflect that this bondage of the body is but temporary.
What is the use of a conquered earth, what is the use of a mountain of gold held in one’s hand,
and what is the use of celestial women, when death has been inscribed by Brahmā?
She lives for only a few moments, yet during those moments she seems to have mastered the sacred scriptures;
in that brief time, she confounds the existing systems and composes new ones.
The duration of life is very short, the intellect is small, and familiarity is slight;
yet we might somehow cross over [this world] if the sacred scriptures did not arise.
I do not know from where you have come, nor do I know where you must go;
where now do you wander upon this path of saṃsāra in its great darkness?
Those enveloped by darkness, wandering nearby or far away, do not perceive objects;
yet fools clearly perceive them when their heads are struck by a flash of lightning.
Here young women blink their eyes, while there young women do not blink;
such indeed is the distinction. What else is there to say of heaven as "heaven"?
Whether it be the wrath of Maitrāvaruṇi or the curse of the sage Tārkṣya,
if even that of an enemy is remembered but once, let there be no station for Indra.
Whether one goes to Amarāvatī or to the city of the Four-Faced One,
if a person must return again, what has been accomplished?
Many wives have been enjoyed, and sons and grandsons have been obtained; even a hundred years of life have been spent. Speak the truth: is there a mind set on dying?
Seeing that sense objects are by nature subject to disintegration, who would conceive the notion of "mine" toward them?
Who would purchase with wealth a horse that has already reached the state of perishing?
"In the absence of food there is death; food comes from rice; rice comes from rain;
rain comes from austerity"—saying this, let him practice that austerity for the sake of immortality.
Why do people not restrain their minds? Why do they not resort to Śiva as their refuge? By the mere absence of ulterior motives, they are not bound even while engaged in the means to liberation.
This body serves for enjoyment to the vulgar and for yoga to the discerning;
yet it is of no use for either enjoyment or yoga to those who are pretentiously clever.
When the Sage spoke of "Brahmins and Caṇḍālas," he did so specifically with reference to those who travel upon the great highway of existence— the great highway of *bhava*.
Among kings, there is one or two; among gods, five or six; and in the case of Brahmā, only five or six:
such are the drops of the ocean of the bliss of Brahman found in this world.
When consciousness is obscured by ignorance, what can karma do?
When the eye is impaired by darkness, what could one see even by opening one's mouth wide?
How is it that people rejoice by relying on the firefly of knowledge, which is exceedingly turbid, fleeting, momentarily flashing, and devoid of any true desirability?
Fools might offer ten thousand or even a million ordinary enjoyments for the sake of material pleasure, yet they do not purchase absolute liberation with even five or six *bilva* leaves.
As long as they continue their activity, the knot remains bound in the snare;
if they proceed with secrecy, the snare will loosen in due time.
These sages obstruct their breaths; they neither eat nor drink.
They are praised by virtuous people—what do they place around their necks? A golden noose.
Granted that people smile when the splendors of Kailāsa are described;
yet they turn their faces away when the means of attainment are explained.
People vainly inquire about regions, asking "How are the Vaṅgas? or "How are the Aṅgas?"; yet no one at all desires to know what the city of Death (Kṛtānta) is like.
The sense of "mine" should be abandoned, provided it can be abandoned; however, if it cannot be abandoned, then the sense of "mine" should instead be applied to everything.
A fool speaks of "sons" and "wives" as those who must be supported;
he does not realize that it is his own self which is sinking into blind darkness while being supported.
Whatever was contemplated within the womb and whatever was long contemplated in hell—
all that was wiped away at once through contact with the winds of the sense-objects.
The activity of the vital breath, characterized by inhalation and exhalation, has its course directed outward;
it drags the activity of the mind away, just as an unchaste woman drags away a simple, virtuous wife.
I beheld the great ocean of consciousness belonging to the Great Beings— extremely deep, untroubled, imperturbable, its further shore unseen and impossible to cross, and agitated by incessant waves.
In order to abandon terrible worldly existence, some take refuge in the Aghora [aspect]; for those terrified by transmigration, the power of Śambhu is the true refuge.
If the bond is to be released, one must approach Paśupati himself;
for animals bound by a bond are certainly not liberated [by anyone else].
Enough, enough with mothers who have already been experienced; and enough with fathers!
If it must be so eternally, let there be [only] the mother and the father.
Blessed are those many gods who have no famine;
we, however, never know that one Lord as full.
Let the gods be great; however, the mind does not strive to bow before them.
According to the logic of the wealthy and the generous, one should contemplate in the mind only the Conqueror of Death.
You contemplate the pleasure of the sense-objects, yet you do not contemplate their bitter ripening;
consider instead that very kinsman who is capable both of binding and of liberating.
The abode is attendance upon the guru; the refuge is the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the five-syllabled mantra;
and the wealth for men dwelling in the final stage of life is the cessation of all longing.
Who are the parents? Who is the son? Who is the master of this phenomenal world?
When duality has subsided, what inquiry can there be as to "What is this? or "What is that? (AppVs_89)
That is the injunction which they perform; that is the prohibition from which they desist;
and that is the secret doctrine which the wise followers of Śiva, who live by their vows, proclaim.
Abandon this essence-less worldly existence; take refuge in the Beloved of Pārvatī.
Have faith in the pinnacle of the Vedas, for this entire universe acts according to your command.
Let the creator of very dull intellect mark us as either capable or incapable;
our refuge and our feet are the left and right feet of Maheśa.
To the question "How is Hari the Creator? How? we are indeed mute;
we know Śiva alone, and we know nothing other than Śiva.
The forest of sword-leaves is dreadful, and the Andhatāmisra hell is most dreadful;
what loss could there be for us from that, since we belong to Śiva, reaching back even to the four-faced Brahmā?

Bharadvāja, who has undergone initiation for the Ghorā sacrifice and stands at the pinnacle of the Kula, is one among the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras); there is no doubt that he is indeed the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).

Thinking, "May there never be a quarrel," the two Śivas, who have attained oneness of body, fell into a dispute over my protection, each crying, "I am [the protector]! I am [the protector]! AppVs_96 //
Some who have taken refuge in the yoga of Maheśvara do not consider even the hells as enjoyments, nor do they regard other gods as anything but the lowest of men.
O child, if it is not possible for one who is not liberated to know, abandon, hear, think, or grasp an object, or to grasp the self, then establish that [liberation].
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the Vedas, devotion, ritual action, and philosophical conviction—
all of these are found together in one place, yet they remain entirely separate in another.
Who will tell you [the truth] while you are bound? One who is liberated knows liberation. If you go to Avimukta, you will know it from the mouth of Viśveśvara.
I have not grasped the heart of the Vedas, nor have I failed to grasp my own wavering heart;
yet I desire to go to the supreme abode, the city of the Lord of the Universe.
Thus ends the *Vairāgyaśataka* composed by the illustrious Appayadīkṣita.
